Serv Safe: 0 Found one squirt bottle of oil that wasn't labeled. All foods and food ingredients that are not readily and unmistakably recognized; such as dry pasta or beans; must be labeled with common name of food. This is especially important with foods such as cooking oils; flour; herbs; salt; spices; and sugar.
Shut-off observed on hose attached to a hose bib with an atmospheric vacuum breaker with the water left on. These mushroom-shaped backflow preventers located at the faucet of a hose bib are not approved for installation with any shut-offs downstream from preventer when under constant pressure. Remove spray guns; valved splitters; or any other shut offs downstream from backflow preventer and/or make sure to turn water off and relieve pressure when sinks are not in use. If such an attachment is necessary at the hose bib or the water must be left on for extended periods of time; contact a plumber for advice on installing an approved backflow preventer. The water at the sink was turned off and pressure was released during inspection.

Many people mix there own sanitizer with solutions like you had in the truck today. Some food trucks purchase spray bottles of ready-made sanitizers such as Redi San RTU Hard Surface Sanitizer (It is a QAC) or Clorox Anywhere Hard Surface Daily Sanitizing Spray (Bleach Water).  It has to be a No Rinse sanitizer approved for food contact surfaces and there must be a test kit for it so the strength can be determined. The ready made products have stabilizers in the solution so they stay the proper strength until the product is used up. If you mix your own they have to be changed at least every day.

Cold holding temperature requirement for potentially hazardous food has changed from 45F to 41F. Points may be deducted for this beginning in 2019. Ready to eat; potentially hazardous foods kept in the establishment more than 24 hours shall be date marked. Date marking should be either a preparation date; or a consume-by date. Establishments may use either a 4 day or 7 day shelf life BASED ON THE ABILITY OF ALL EQUIPMENT IN THE ESTABLISHMENT TO HOLD FOODS AT 41 DEGREES F OR BELOW. Strongly recommend a 4 day shelf life until person in charge can document a track record of all equipment holding foods at 41 F or below. Certain foods; such as cultured milk products; some cheeses; commercially packed deli salads; and some cured or dried meats are exempt from this requirement. Contact your inspector if you have questions about whether a specific item must be date marked. Replace sanitizer test strips which have become wet and no longer test concentration correctly. Reminder: clean; sanitize; and air dry coolers used for direct food contact (tortillas).

Serv Safe: 0 The health inspector must designate the location for posting the grade card. The grade card must be located in a conspicuous place where it may be readily observed by the public upon entering the food establishment. If the person in charge of the food establishment objects to the location designated by the health inspector then the person in charge may suggest an alternative location which meets the criteria of this Rule. (b) When an inspection of a food establishment is made; the regulatory authority shall remove the existing grade card; issue a new grade card; and post the new grade card in the same location where the grade card was previously posted as long as that location remains conspicuous. The person in charge of the food establishment must keep the grade card posted at the designated location at all times. The grade card may be posted in another location which meets the criteria of this Rule if agreed upon by the person in charge and the health inspector. Follow-Up: 02/06/2017

Serv Safe: 0 Upon arrival for inspection; inspector washed hands at only hand sink in kitchen/prep area and noticed it was causing standing water onto floor. After investigating; it was noted that the floor drain underneath the handwashing sink and prep sink was clogged and actively backing up onto the floor. Inspector then turned water on at the three compartment sink and started a cycle on the dish machine; as these are tied into a separate floor drain. The floor drain supplying the 3 compartment sink and dish machine did NOT back up when in use. Per the PIC; a plumber had been contacted; but was unable to repair this until after the holiday. Inspector advised PIC to contact a plumber immediately; or a suspension of the permit would need to be issued until the repair has been completed. Inspector then advised all food preparation to cease until repairs have been made. Plumber then arrived to facility prior to the end of inspection to make repairs. Once repairs were completed; inspector assessed the area. Floor drain; per plumber; was clogged and something lodged in the piping. The floor drain is now functioning properly. Inspector advised PIC to wash; rinse; and sanitize entire 3 compartment sink; prep sink area; floors that were affected as well as discard vegetables that were sitting in the standing water. .15A NCAC 18A .2661 A request for reinspection for the purpose of raising the alphabetical grade may be made once critical violations have been corrected. The regulatory authority shall make an unannounced inspection within 15 days from the date of the request. Serv Safe: 0 Reviewed employee health policy during inspection and most of the basic information is correct; however; 1 illnesses listed is not specific enough to comply with NC Food Code requirements. On document available in facility; only E.coli is listed; in order to comply with Food Code; E.coli 0157:H7; Enterohemorrhagic (ETEC) and Shiga toxin-producing (STEC) E. coli must be listed. Additionally; the FDA has added nontyphiodal Salmonella as an illness that is be included in the illness that need to be reported. Policy needs to be updated to include the specific illnesses. The policy also does not include restriction or exclusion time (24-48 hours depending on symptoms/illness); this information should be added to policy so that employees are fully aware how long that have to be out of work if they report foodborne illness symptoms or are diagnosed with a foodborne illness.

Serv Safe: 0 *During inspection; quat sanitizer solution was in the 3 compartment sink but was not actively being used however; the solution being dispensed for the sink was only 70F. According to NC Food Code [4-501.114(C)(1)]; quat sanitizer solution shall be at least 75F. The dispenser is currently plumbed directly into the cold water line. A mixing valve of some type needs to be installed so that the solution is dispensed at required temperatures or documentation stating that the particular product used in this facility is effective below 75F must be provided.
The 2013 FDA Food Code has added nontyphiodal Salmonella as an illness that is be included in the illness that need to be reported. This is currently not being enforced in NC and is not a violation at this time. This provided for information purposes only; should operator choose to update their existing policy.

Serv Safe: 0 At start of inspection; the foods in the walk-in cooler were all holding above 45F. Just prior to start of inspection; the cooler had been frequently opened and held open while foods were being removed for preparation. It also appeared that the cooler may have been going through a defrost cycle. The cooler was left closed and within 30 minutes foods in the cooler had dropped about 2 degrees and by end of inspection all foods were holding below 45F. When preparing for the start of the day; avoid leaving the cooler door open as much as possible but it is also recommended to have your refrigeration company check when the unit is defrosting. Defrosting should occur during slow periods or while the restaurant is closed so that the cooler is not stressed and foods will be maintained at proper temperatures at all times.

Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; observed good hand washing and good use of no bare hand contact with ready to eat foods. However; employees on the cooking line were observed wearing gloves while using utensils to cook and handle other foods when not needed. Gloves are not required to be worn if foods can be handled with tongs; spoons; or other utensils. When gloves are not worn properly; it can actually increase risk of cross-contamination. Gloves are only required to be used when ready to eat food is handled without a utensil or other barrier. Recommend using different colored gloves if wearing gloves for handling and preparing raw meat.

Items shall then be air dried on right drain board or on clean shelving/table. Train workers on proper washing; rinsing and santizing of food equipment and utensils. Follow-Up: 07/20/2023

Serv Safe: 0 According to information given by PIC; facility is engaging in par cooking/non-continuous cooking of chicken; however; the chicken observed during inspection was fully cooked. EHS strongly encourages fully cooking the chicken instead of using a non-continuous cooking process.

Serv Safe: 0 At the mop sink; a hose with a spray gun is hooked up to the faucet which is being left on when the hose is not in use; this can create a pressure build up and damage the atmospheric vacuum breaker (AVB) because it is not rated to be under constant pressure. Make sure to turn off the water and release the pressure on the hose or dispenser or installed secondary; pressure-rated backflow prevention. The water was turned off and pressure was released during inspection.

Serv Safe: 0 On the bake side; the quat sanitizer solution was only 68F. According to instructions on the quat test strips and NC Food Code; quat solution should be maintain at a minimum of 75F. The solution temperature can affect both the efficacy of the solution and how the test strips react. Water that is too cool can cause the test strips to give a false low. The solution was changed and corrected during inspection.

Serv Safe: 0 Observed burgers being assembled and wrapped for hot holding but cold cheese slices were being placed onto the burgers; bringing down the temperature. It is recommended to remove just enough sliced cheese for the amount of burgers/sandwiches needed from the cooler and allow it to temper so that it is not so cold when going onto the burgers. This may be a good opportunity for use of Time as a Public Health Control (TPHC); which would allow food to be out for up to 4 hours without temperature control; however; any food not used within the time limit specified would have to be discarded at the end of the allotted time frame. TPHC can be utilized for any food product; as long as written procedures are in place prior to starting it and the procedures are available for review during inspection. Discussed TPHC with manager.

Serv Safe: 0 Upon arrival; staff was on lunch break so no food was being handled or prepared. Observed 1 sanitizer bucket under the prep sink that tested too weak with test strips. PIC stated the solution was from the 3 compartment sink; which tested properly; however a dry cotton rag had been placed into the fresh solution after it was taken out of the sink. The dry cotton rag will bind up the sanitizer chemical and cause it to be out of solution; resulting in low or no sanitizer concentration. Cotton rags should be dampened; either with sanitizer solution or plain water; prior to being placed into the sanitizer solution; if using plain water; rags should be rung out to remove excess water that could dilute solution.
Make sure to turn off the water at the mop sink when the sink is not in active use to prevent damage to the vacuum breaker and possible damage to the plumbing system.

Discussed this with GM and kitchen manager. EHS will send information on non-continuous cooking approval and procedures by email.

Serv Safe: 0 EDUCATIONAL NOTE ABOUT PROPER DATE MARKING:  Ready to eat; potentially hazardous foods (PHF) kept in the establishment more than 24 hours shall be date marked. This includes canned PHF put in different containers; on-site prepared potentially hazardous salads; opened deli meat packages; cartons of milk; etc.  Date marking should be either a preparation date or a consume-by date.  Establishments may use either a 7 day shelf life BASED ON THE ABILITY OF ALL EQUIPMENT IN THE ESTABLISHMENT TO HOLD FOODS AT 41 DEGREES F OR BELOW or a 4 day shelf life if equipment can only hold foods between 41F and 45F.  Strongly recommend a 4 day shelf life until person in charge can document a track record of all equipment holding foods at 41 degrees F or below.   Certain foods; such as cultured milk products; some cheeses; commercially packed deli salads; and some cured or dried meats are exempt from this requirement.   Contact your inspector if you have questions about whether a specific food must be date marked.

Serv Safe: 0 COOLING ISSUES: Observed a large plastic bag over a speed rack with condensation on the inside of bag; indicating that food was possibly still quite warm when food was covered. Plastic bags can easily trap in the heat; preventing rapid chilling...Also observed very large pieces of wrapped cooked roasts (one up to 12 inches+ in diameter) that were in freezer. Ensure these roasts are cooled properly from 135F to 70F within 2 hours and from 70F to 45/41F or less within 4 additional hours. Use a calibrated thermometer to check food temperatures. Use a time/temperature chart to log the cooling of these roasts to ensure they are cooling properly. If roasts are not cooling properly; then they need to be cut into small pieces--such as 4 inch pieces--so they can cool more rapidly...PROCEDURE FOR PAR-COOKING OF RAW ANIMAL FOODS SUCH AS SAUSAGES: Must follow established written procedure; including date marking; proper storing; etc. Today; did not observed that par-cooked sausages were marked that they had been par-cooked.

Serv Safe: 0 ISSUES REGARDING TIME AS PUBLIC HEALTH CONTROL:  If time as a public health control will be used for certain potentially hazardous foods; a time control sheet (previously given to manager) must be completed for each food and food must be properly labeled according to the sheet. This is not a direct violation of NC Food Code but high temperatures can cause the testing strips; that are used to check the concentration; to react incorrectly and cause a false high sanitizer concentration reading. Quat sanitizer should be at around 75-110F for proper testing. It is recommended to either install a mixing valve at the water line so that the temperature is regulated or have a valve installed on the faucet that will allow for the temperature to be manually adjusted.

Serv Safe: 0 3-603.11 Consumption of Animal Foods that are Raw; Undercooked; or Not Otherwise Processed to Eliminate Pathogens - Establishment found to offer at least one undercooked animal-based food and has insufficient consumer advisory. Consumer advisory shall be provided for any undercooked animal-based food with the exception of some steaks. Consumer advisory must consist of a disclosure; wherein the name of the food on the menu indicates that it may be served undercooked; such as “Hamburger (cooked to order);” and the disclosure must be asterisked to a reminder stating the following: “Consuming raw or undercooked meats; poultry; seafood; shellfish; or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness.” (Two alternate statements are available; ask your inspector if you have questions.) Please contact your inspector with any questions about this rule; or to have proposed wording approved before modifying menu. Follow-Up: 11/01/2012

Serv Safe: 0 Upon assessing menu and speaking to PIC regarding processes; PIC stated that the facility uses a 4 hour sous vide method for the whole muscle intact steaks provided on the menu. After product sous vides to ~130 F; an ice bath is used to cool product. It is cooled to 41 F and when ordered the package is first opened to sear the steak to order. Facility is sous viding these products in the original packaging rather than creating a reduced oxygen environment by vacuum sealing on site. Also; inspector discovered the facility is cooking pork on outside grill about once a month. Facility places pork on grill first; then finishes in the oven. After it is removed from the inside oven; it is picked; portioned; and cooled. Product is reheated once product is ordered by customer. Inspector provided guidance on both of these processes to ensure proper procedures are followed moving forward.

Please find the current North Carolina Food Code Manual at the following URL: https://www.wakegov.com/departments-government/environmental-health-safety/rules-and-resources  Hand Hygiene Program Requirements listed below: Food employees not serving a highly susceptible population may contact exposed; ready-to-eat food with their bare hands if: (1) The permit holder obtains prior approval from the regulatory authority; (2) Written procedures are maintained in the food establishment and made available to the regulatory authority upon request that include: (a) For each bare hand contact procedure; a listing of the specific ready-to-eat foods that are touched by bare hands; (b) Diagrams and other information showing that handwashing facilities; installed; located; equipped; and maintained as specified under sec.sec. 5-203.11; 5-204.11; 5-205.11; 6-301.11; 6-301.12; and 6-301.14; are in an easily accessible location and in close proximity to the work station where the bare hand contact procedure is conducted; (3) A written employee health policy that details how the food establishment complies with sec.sec. 2-201.11; 2-201.12; and 2-201.13 including: (a) Documentation that food employees and conditional employees acknowledge that they are informed to report information about their health and activities as they relate to gastrointestinal symptoms and diseases that are transmittable through food as specified under par. 2-201.11(A); (b) Documentation that food employees and conditional employees acknowledge their responsibilities as specified under par. 2-201.11(E) and (F); and (c) Documentation that the person in charge acknowledges the responsibilities as specified under par.par. 2-201.11(B); (C) and (D); and sec.sec. 2-201.12 and 2-201.13; (4) Documentation that food employees acknowledge that they have received training in: (a) The risks of contacting the specific ready-to-eat foods with bare hands; (b) Proper handwashing as specified under sec. 2-301.12; (c) When to wash their hands as specified under sec. 2-301.14; (d) Where to wash their hands as specified under sec. 2-301.15; (e) Proper fingernail maintenance as specified under sec. 2-302.11; (f) Prohibition of jewelry as specified under sec. 2-303.11; and (g) Good hygienic practices as specified under sec.sec.2-401.11 and 2-401.12; (5) Documentation that hands are washed before food preparation and as necessary to prevent cross contamination by food employees as specified under sec.sec. 2-301.11; 2-301.12; 2-301.14; and 2-301.15 during all hours of operation when the specific ready-to-eat foods are prepared; (6) Documentation that food employees contacting ready-to-eat food with bare hands use two or more of the following control measures to provide additional safeguards to hazards associated with bare hand contact: (a) Double handwashing; (b) Nail brushes; (c) A hand antiseptic after handwashing as specified under sec. 2-301.16; (d) Incentive programs such as paid sick leave that assist or encourage food employees not to work when they are ill; or (e) Other control measures approved by the regulatory authority; and (7) Documentation that corrective action is taken when Subparagraphs (E) (1) - (6) of this section are not followed.

Serv Safe: 0 *Notice* Effective January 1; 2019; the NC Food Code 3-501.16 (A)(2)(b)(ii) NOW requires equipment to be upgraded or replaced to maintain food at a temperature of 41 degrees F or less. If you have any questions/concerns; please feel free to call 919-868-6416 or email meghan.scott@wakegov.com   NOTE: All potentially hazardous food must now be held at 41F or below. Points will be deducted on the next inspection if this violation continues. If cold-holding equipment is unable to maintain foods at 41F or below; equipment should be assessed by a professional to determine if the unit needs cleaning; repair; recharge; etc. Settings of unit should be assessed to determine if cooler can be set to a lower temperature. Food container should not block fans inside cooler and space should be allowed around containers to create cold air flow. Hot foods should not be placed in prep coolers next to foods that are already cold. Metal pans and lids should be used where possible. Keep lids on prep cooler closed as much as possible. Foods such as tomatoes; melons; and canned foods should be chilled before they are cut or prepared. Minimize the time that foods are held out of refrigeration for prep. If the unit still cannot hold foods at 41F or below; consider replacing the unit or only holding non-potentially hazardous foods in that unit or holding foods according to a time limit. Contact EHS for more details on holding food by time limits.   Complaint ID 8773259

NOTE: Reach-in freezer observed to be higher than freezing temperatures. Food inside measured at 41F or below but observed to be defrosting. Please monitor this freezer to ensure proper function. All potentially hazardous food must now be held at 41F or below. If cold-holding equipment is unable to maintain foods at 41F or below; equipment should be assessed by a professional to determine if the unit needs cleaning; repair; recharge; gasket repair; etc. Compressor fans should not be blocked by other equipment. Food should be arranged inside the unit to allow air flow around the interior. The ambient air temperature of the kitchen should not exceed manufacturer recommendations for proper function of coolers. Settings of unit should be assessed to determine if cooler can be set to a lower temperature. Hot foods should not be placed in prep coolers next to foods that are already cold; cool foods to 41F before placing them in prep coolers. Metal pans and lids should be used where possible. Minimize the time that foods are held out of refrigeration for prep. Temperatures in all refrigeration units should be taken and recorded daily to determine temperature patterns. If the unit still cannot hold foods at 41F or below; consider replacing the unit or only holding non-potentially hazardous foods in that unit or holding foods according to a time limit. Serv Safe: 0 Facility receives pizza delivered from Domino's; which Iceplex employees distribute to birthday party clients along with cake and ice cream. No snack bar food present at time of inspection to check hot or cold holding temperatures (only in freezer). Employees may not touch any ready-to-eat foods with bare hands. Employees shall use gloves; utensils; deli papers; etc. in lieu of bare-hand contact. As a reminder; employees shall wash their hands before putting on gloves and at any glove change. Gloves shall be changed when switching between raw and cooked foods; after cleaning activities; after touching hair or face; and after any other activities that may soil gloves. Ready to eat; potentially hazardous foods kept in the establishment more than 24 hours past opening or preparation shall be date marked. Date marking should be either a preparation date; or a consume-by date. Establishments may use either a 4 day or 7 day shelf life BASED ON THE ABILITY OF ALL EQUIPMENT IN THE ESTABLISHMENT TO HOLD FOODS AT 41 DEGREES F OR BELOW. Strongly recommend a 4 day shelf life until person in charge can document a track record of all equipment holding foods at 41 F or below. Certain foods; such as cultured milk products; some cheeses; commercially packed deli salads; and some cured or dried meats are exempt from this requirement. Contact your inspector if you have questions about whether a specific item must be date marked. Replace missing ceiling tiles in janitor's closet.  Follow-Up: 12/25/2012

Serv Safe: 0 Due to the repeat violations of #22; cold holding of TCS foods at 41F or below; a risk control plan shall be implemented for the next two weeks. The facility has a line check that they have begun performing that includes checks for cold holding; hot holding; & reheating. This check is performed twice a day; once at 1030 and once at 1600; every day. The log for this check shall be sent to the REHS until at least 08.02.2024. Methods discussed for improvement include: a larger amount of ice surrounding the pans; cooling all product in the walk-in prior to placing it on ice; not overfilling these pans; and placing food further back inside of the refrigerated drawers. If improvement is not seen; then additional measures may need to be implemented such as replacing this ice rail system with actual cold-holding units that can maintain food in a properly chilled ambient environment. If you have any questions/concerns; please feel free to call 919-868-6416 or email meghan.scott@wakegov.com  CFPM Terri Crocker Exp 1/22/24  NOTE: All potentially hazardous food must now be held at 41F or below. If cold-holding equipment is unable to maintain foods at 41F or below; equipment should be assessed by a professional to determine if the unit needs cleaning; repair; recharge; gasket repair; etc. Compressor fans should not be blocked by other equipment. Food should be arranged inside the unit to allow air flow around the interior. The ambient air temperature of the kitchen should not exceed manufacturer recommendations for proper function of coolers. Settings of unit should be assessed to determine if cooler can be set to a lower temperature. Hot foods should not be placed in prep coolers next to foods that are already cold; cool foods to 41F before placing them in prep coolers. Metal pans and lids should be used where possible. Foods such as tomatoes; melons; and canned foods should be chilled before they are cut or prepared. Foods should not be overfilled in containers (keep below fill lines in pans). Minimize the time that foods are held out of refrigeration for prep. Temperatures in all refrigeration units should be taken and recorded daily to determine temperature patterns. If the unit still cannot hold foods at 41F or below; consider replacing the unit or only holding non-potentially hazardous foods in that unit or holding foods according to a time limit. Contact EHS for more details on holding food by time limits.   NOTE: Organization of storage room has improved significantly. Organization in reach-in cooler has improved. Excellent handwashing observed. Follow-Up: 05/10/2019

Serv Safe: 0 **NOTE** For marinara sauce held warm; If sauce is made that day from a can; it should be heated to 135F then placed on the steam well and held at 135F or above. The sauce may be cooled by following these steps: Spread sauce into several shallow pans. Date mark all pans. When sauce reaches 135F; place sauce in the walk-in cooler. Cover sauce loosely (allow heat to escape from the container). Stir sauce occasionally while it cools. Sauce should cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours and from 70F to 41F within 4 hours (6 hours overall). If the sauce does not cool according to these requirements; it should be discarded. The next day; this sauce should be heated to 165F before being placed on the steam well and held at 135F or above. *Notice* Effective January 1; 2019; the NC Food Code 3-501.16 (A)(2)(b)(ii) NOW requires equipment to be upgraded or replaced to maintain food at a temperature of 41 degrees F or less. Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; dishes were being cleaned and sanitized in the dish machine but the 3 compartment sink was being set up and the quat sanitizing solution was being dispensed at 53F. NC Food Code requires a minimum temperature of 75F for quat sanitizers. At 53F the solution was registering around 400 ppm and PIC stated that they usually dilute the solution using hot water to bring the temperature up to 75F and lower the concentration to around 200 ppm. As long as the solution is being used at the correct minimum temperature and the concentration meets minimum requirements; methods used by this facility are allowed but it is recommended to have a mixing valve installed so that the solution temperature is regulated at 75-110F and hot water does not have to be added manually to dilute the sanitizing solutions.
At the automatic handsink next to the dish area; the water temperature cannot be manually adjusted and was reaching 130F. This temperature can cause scalding and does not allow for proper handwashing. The water temperature needs to be adjusted so that it is at least 100F but does not exceed 120F. Ideal handwashing temperature is 110-115F.

Serv Safe: 0 At start of inspection; the water from the automatic mixing faucet on the handsink by the dish pit was 126F. This is too hot to properly handwash. The mixing valve below the sink was adjusted during inspection and the temperature was brought down to 106F. Hot water at handsinks must be at least 100F but should not exceed 120F.

Serv Safe: 0 Establishment has proposed using AUTODONER Vertical Broilers for cooking chicken. Serv Safe: 0 Lamb Gyro Procedures  Definition: Gyro is a cone of seasoned restructured; ground raw meat. ?	All meat are obtained and inspected from approved source. ?	Meat cone comes in frozen. Must be kept frozen until ready to be cooked.  Cooking Instructions:  ?	Remove frozen meat cone from the freezer; mount on Skewer pit and place directly on the rotating vertical broiler. ?	Once the exterior of the meat cone is cooked; (use thermometer probe temperature should reach 165°) using a clean; sanitized knife; slice approximately    ¼ inch thick slices.  Meat must be cooked completely before storing in the warmer; it may need to be cooked on the grill so that the inside surface also reaches 165° ?	Sliced cooked meat then held in a (warmer) heat unit at 145° until ready to serve.  During busy lunch or special events ?	Gyro meat is sliced off the cone (according to instruction above).  After all parts reach at least 165° temperature including being cooked on the grill; cut to small pieces; then held in a warmer at 145°; ready to serve. ?	Gyro cone will be continuously cooked no more than 2-3 hours. ?	Fully Cooked Gyros Slices may be cooled in a shallow metal pan; spread out  (only 2 inches high); then cooled uncovered in a refrigerator to below 45°.  After the cooling process it can be covered & stacked (or combined).

Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; it was observed that the dish sink chemical dispensers are plumbed directly into a hot water line. The sanitizer solution in the sink during inspection was 123F. Hot water used for sanitizer can effect the accuracy of test strips and is too hot to safely put hands into to remove dishes from the sink after sanitizing. EHS recommended having a mixing valve installed at the sink to allow for manual adjustment of the water temperature for the chemical dispenser. The soap used must be at least 110F and the sanitizer must be at least 75F but the recommended temperature range for test strip accuracy and safety is 75-110F.

Serv Safe: 0 **NOTE** According to PIC; butter is held at room temperature during service. Butter is held in squeeze bottles for ease of use. Butter is held near the heat lamps at the line to maintain a creamy and malleable texture. Butter is heated as needed per bottle. Usually remainder of butter is discarded at the end of the night (5pm-10pm). Each bottle usually lasts no longer than 2-3 hours. However; a bottle was held in an undercounter cooler during the inspection which according to PIC was heated last night for service and placed back in the cooler after closing. No softened butter observed in the kitchen during inspection. Because butter is considered to be a potentially hazardous food; if it is held at room temperature it should be held using Time as a Public Health Control (procedure used for bearnaise sauce). Under this procedure; the butter may be held out of the cooler for a maximum of 4 hours. After 4 hours; the butter must be discarded. Butter may never be saved for use the next day or put in other recipes or dishes. If the 4 total hours is not used at the end of the night (example: butter softened at 9pm and facility closes at 10:30pm); the butter must still be discarded and may not be saved. Butter should be time marked with the time it is removed from the cooler. Written procedures must be held onsite (see emailed form; same form as used with bearnaise sauce). Please contact Meghan Scott 919-868-6416; meghan.scott@wakegov.com with any questions about this procedure.    *Notice* Effective January 1; 2019; the NC Food Code 3-501.16 (A)(2)(b)(ii) NOW requires equipment to be upgraded or replaced to maintain food at a temperature of 41 degrees F or less. Serv Safe: 0 Facility has started cooking and cooling spaghetti noodles. The noodles are cooked; cooled under running cold water; then bagged and frozen. Recommend adding ice while rinsing the noodles in cold water and leaving the bags open after portioning to allow any residual heat to escape. Also; remember to date mark the noodles on the date that they are prepared then the date they are pulled from the freezer to thaw. The preparation date is Day 1; the pull/thaw date is Day 2. If the noodles are maintained at 41F or less; they can be held for up to 7 days. If held between 41F and 45F; the noodles can only be held for 4 days.

Serv Safe: 0 We discussed COOLING of chicken today.  Hot chicken going into the freezer has caused some problems. It is acceptable to have chicken briefly stored at room temperature. We looked at handouts and discussed that cooling effectiveness is measured by food temperature. Chicken temperature starts around 200 degrees. From the time any part of the food reaches 135F; it shall be 70F or colder in less than 2 hours.  Chicken should be spread out into shallow layers on metal pans; spaced on speed rack; uncovered or loosely covered. Use your thermometer. Cooling may start with food stored at room temperature (outside the walk-in cooler).  Check food temperature and make sure that it is not between 135F and 70F for more than 2 hours.

Serv Safe: 0 During the inspection today I found out that the establishment had been buying raw chicken from a grocery store and bringing it here to be prepped and cooked. This was not observed today during the inspection only discussed. This facility was permitted to have all their meat and poultry come in pre-cooked and has been permitted as a Category 2 restaurant. Therefore; by performing this action the establishment is in violation of their permit. Approval has not been given and the facility does not have the proper equipment to prepare and cook raw chicken. The establishment was told to immediately stop purchasing raw chicken to cook and sell. Other options have been discussed to purchase chicken that is already cooked. A follow-up visit will be done to ensure that the establishment is no longer buying raw chicken. If the establishment wishes to buy raw chicken and cook it within the establishment plan review will NEED TO BE CONTACTED FIRST.

Serv Safe: 0 Educational note:  Rice observed soaking in water at room temperature in preparation for grinding. Strongly recommend that this process be done in walk in cooler for any length of soaking; and this process must be done under refrigeration if soaking time will last more than four hours. Educational note:  Ensure that employees wash hands when changing tasks or doing any activities that would contaminate the hands; including after taking dirty wares to the dish area.   PLEASE NOTE:  Container of rice observed at 50 degrees F on prep counter.  PIC states that it is awaiting reheating and immediately began reheating process.  Please minimize the amount of time that foods sit out while awaiting reheating.  If reheating space is limited; foods awaiting reheating should be kept in cooler until space is available.

Serv Safe: 0 Educational note: Good compliance with health notification and management decision trees. Per PIC question: An employee with sore throat and fever would be required to be RESTRICTED in duties until cleared by a doctor (Reinstate a FOOD EMPLOYEE who was EXCLUDED or RESTRICTED as specified under Subparagraphs 2-201.12(G)(1) or (2) if the FOOD EMPLOYEE provides to the PERSON IN CHARGE written medical documentation from a HEALTH PRACTITIONER stating that the FOOD EMPLOYEE meets one of the following conditions:(1) Has received antibiotic therapy for Streptococcus pyogenes infection for more than 24 hours;(2) Has at least one negative throat specimen culture for Streptococcus pyogenes infection; or(3) Is otherwise determined by a HEALTH PRACTITIONER to be free of a Streptococcus pyogenes infection.) Sore throat with fever is NOT required to be reported to the health department; nor does an employee have a responsibility to report exposure to someone with those symptoms. No evidence of any violations associated with this guidance. Please note: consumer advisory clearly discloses which items (eggs cooked to order) may be undercooked; and reminds consumers of the risk of eating such eggs. Recommend that phrasing be changed from "could cause foodborne illness" to "may increase your risk of foodborne illness." The latter wording is the accepted standard.

Serv Safe: 0 Discussed cooling of chicken and chicken broth during inspection. Chicken broth was being cooled by placing a large bucket type container on the prep sink drainboard with an ice wand; it appeared to be reaching required cooling parameters but it is recommended to either cool the broth using the ice wand in an ice bath or in the freezer. Recommend spreading the chicken out on a sheet pan or separating it out into 2 containers to lessen the thickness of the food.   Also discussed labeling on portioned chicken salad for sale as a "grab and go" item. Foods that are available for customer self-service must be properly labeled as follows: 1) common name of the food 2) list of the food ingredients; if more than 2 ingredients; in descending order 3) accurate declaration of the quantities 4) name and place of business where the food was made; packaged; and/or distributed 5) the name of the food source of each major allergen container in the food unless the source is already in the common name of the food; they were not being used during inspection; but the Red Bull and Pepsi coolers in the dining room are not approved for foods that are packaged in the restaurant. Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; EHS observed a sink with soap and paper towels; like a handsink; being used to dump coffee. Manager stated that this was used as a handsink and dump sink due to observations made during a previous inspecting in which catering prep was being done in the back corner of the facility. This area is no longer being used for catering or any food prep whatsoever; only dry storage. Since catering is not longer done and the coffee and tea station does not need handwashing set up; the sink may be used for dumping and the soap and paper towel dispenser should be removed.
At the 3 compartment sink; the quat sanitizer dispenser is plumbed into the hot water line and sanitizer solution is dispensed at greater than 120F. This is not a violation according to the NC Food Code but the high temperature could cause the quat test strips to inaccurately measure the chemical concentration due to a reaction to the heat. the sign posted at the sink; by the chemical supplier; states that the solution should be measured when it is between 65F and 75F; NC Food Code specifies a minimum of 75F unless manufacturer specifications state otherwise. A mixing valve may need to be installed to bring the water temperature down.

Serv Safe: 0 TCS* foods: Time-temperature control for safety foods...CFPM: Robert Ainsworth; Exp. 6-2-2027...DISCUSSION: Live animals are allowed inside a food service establishment in the following situations if the owner or operator does not permit animals to physically contact FOOD; serving dishes; UTENSILS; tableware; LINENS; unwrapped SINGLE-SERVICE and SINGLE-USE ARTICLES or other FOOD service items that may result in contamination of FOOD or FOOD-CONTACT SURFACES and does not permit animals to physically contact EMPLOYEES engaged in the preparation or handling of FOOD:  (1) FISH or crustacea in aquariums or display tanks; (2) Patrol dogs accompanying police or security officers in offices and dining; sales; and storage areas; and sentry dogs in outside fenced areas; (3) SERVICE ANIMALS accompanying persons with disabilities in areas that are not used for FOOD preparation; (4) Dogs and cats in outdoor dining areas; provided that dogs and cats are physically restrained; and do not pass through any indoor areas of the FOOD ESTABLISHMENT. Except for SERVICE ANIMALS described in Subparagraph (3) of this Paragraph; nothing in this Rule prohibits a FOOD ESTABLISHMENT from prohibiting dogs and cats in outdoor dining areas; and  (5) In areas that are not used for FOOD preparation; storage; sales; display; or dining; in which there are caged animals or animals that are similarly confined; such as in a variety store that sells pets or a tourist park that displays animals.

Serv Safe: 0 *NOTE:* Recommend that food placed on salad and hot bars be held using Time as a Public Health Control procedures. Currently; facility cooks food; then holds food in hot cabinets and reach-in coolers at required temperatures until lunch. At 11am; food is placed on the bars for lunch service. Facility checks temperatures of food throughout lunch. After lunch ends at 1:30pm; all food that was held on the bars is discarded. Facility may either choose to 1) Fill out the TPHC procedure form and ensure all food is discarded within 4 hours of placement on bars. This ensures that food on the bars may be held at any temperature without violation during inspections. OR facility may choose to 2) Continue their current process and have temperatures of foods on bars taken during inspections. Under this option; hot foods must be held 135F or above and cold foods must be held 41F or below. Any foods outside these temperatures may result in a violation and/or points deduction. High recommend option 1; filling out the TPHC form and keeping it on the cork board in the office. **NOTE:** Facility occasionally cooks a roast for lunch. No consumer advisory is provided on the menu. Unknown what temperature and how long the roast is held at final cook temperature. Please look into final roast cooking process and contact EHS with the final interior cooking temperature and how long the roast remains at that temperature. Cooking chart for roasts is included in the email to PIC for reference.    *Notice* Effective January 1; 2019; the NC Food Code 3-501.16 (A)(2)(b)(ii) NOW requires equipment to be upgraded or replaced to maintain food at a temperature of 41 degrees F or less. Serv Safe: 0 Drinks are prepared in back customer area at two tables which were pushed together and not in use during inspection. Drinks must only be prepared in approved areas (i.e. bar or kitchen) because these areas are equipped with required hand sinks. Grill on patio is not approved for facility cooking food for customers (no violation observed).   Ready to eat; potentially hazardous foods kept in the establishment more than 24 hours past opening or preparation shall be date marked. Date marking should be either a preparation date; or a consume-by date. Establishments may use either a 4 day or 7 day shelf life BASED ON THE ABILITY OF ALL EQUIPMENT IN THE ESTABLISHMENT TO HOLD FOODS AT 41 DEGREES F OR BELOW. Strongly recommend a 4 day shelf life until person in charge can document a track record of all equipment holding foods at 41 F or below. Certain foods; such as cultured milk products; some cheeses; commercially packed deli salads; and some cured or dried meats are exempt from this requirement. Contact your inspector if you have questions about whether a specific item must be date marked.   Quick reference for guidance on managing sick employees:  http://bit.ly/12q07tm. Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; discussed Peking duck handling and preparation process with PIC. Raw ducks were observed hanging over the meat prep sink after being thawed and seasoned. The ducks were observed to be 74F. PIC stated that the ducks are thawed and then stuffed with spices then quickly blanched in boiling water to make the skin plump up then the ducks are hung at the sink for about 30 minutes to air dry before being placed into the roasting oven to cook. PIC stated that the total time from the thawing process until ducks are placed into oven for cooking is about 2 hours. EHS observed potential issues of cross contamination when the ducks were carried from the sink to the blanching water and then back to the sink; it was recommended to the PIC that a rack or other means of transporting all of the ducks to blanching instead of having to carry them back and forth through the kitchen. EHS will follow up with PIC on this process and safe handling practices.

Serv Safe: 0 *Notice* Effective January 1; 2019; the NC Food Code 3-501.16 (A)(2)(b)(ii) NOW requires equipment to be upgraded or replaced to maintain food at a temperature of 41 degrees F or less. If you have any questions/concerns; please feel free to call 919-868-6416 or email meghan.scott@wakegov.com   NOTE: All potentially hazardous foods must now be held at 41F or below. If cold-holding equipment is unable to maintain foods at 41F or below; equipment should be assessed by a professional to determine if the unit needs cleaning; repair; recharge; etc. Settings of unit should be assessed to determine if cooler can be set to a lower temperature. Hot foods should not be placed in prep coolers next to foods that are already cold. Metal pans and lids should be used where possible. Do not fill pans above fill line (line where pan indents below rim). Foods such as tomatoes; melons; and canned foods should be chilled before they are cut or prepared. Minimize the time that foods are held out of refrigeration for prep. If the unit still cannot hold foods at 41F or below; consider replacing the unit or only holding non-potentially hazardous foods in that unit or holding foods according to a time limit. Contact EHS for more details on holding food by time limits.

FYI: Our rules require you to have a sanitizer and the strength must be able to be verified. I don't know of a test kit for the Purell Foodservice Surface Sanitizer. There is no problem with using it. The pink quat sanitizer solution you have is fine if it is mixed correctly and the temperature should be 70 degrees or above.   Keep a spray bottle or bucket of properly mixed sanitizer such as 50-200 parts per million (ppm) bleach water or 200-400 ppm quaternary ammonia compound (QAC). You could purchase spray bottles of ready-made sanitizers such as Redi San RTU Hard Surface Sanitizer (it is a QAC) or Clorox Anywhere Hard Surface Daily Sanitizing Spray (Bleach Water). The ready made sanitizers have stabilizers mixed in so they don't loose strength.  QAC also comes in tablet form. Usually 1-2 tablets per gallon.  There should be QAC test strips for quaternary ammonia compound products and chlorine test strips for bleach water products. Some places use spray bottles and paper towels or buckets and cloth towels are fine. It doesn't always have to be made up but you have to have the ability to make it if needed.

Serv Safe: 0 During inspection; a final cook temperature was taken on catfish fillets. These are a new product and some pieces are thicker than others. When the cook was taking the temperature on the fish; EHS observed only a few pieces being checked; these pieces were thinner than others. The temperature was exceeding 165F on the thin pieces; however; EHS checked some thicker pieces and found the temperature only reaching 112 degrees on some pieces. The fish was put back into the oven to continue cooking. EHS advised cafeteria staff to be sure and check thicker pieces of fish; in addition to the thinner pieces to insure proper cooking. The labeling on the catfish is unclear as to whether or not the fish is fully cooked; it only says oven-ready and give instructions to cook the fish to at least 145F; which is just above the 140F final cook temperature for seafood. CNS standard requires 165F as a cook temperature for almost all foods.
The dry storage room dunnage racks need to be flipped so that the open side is facing outward to facilitate easier cleaning on the floors.

Serv Safe: 0 Sanitation Grade card missing from Delivery window.  Sanitation grade card in dining area was covered by coffee mugs.  Sanitation grade Cards shall be visible to the public at all times.  Management shall be responsible for maintaining the sanitation grade card in such a  manner that the Grade Card is visible at all times and is maintained at the location where the Environmental Health Specialist posted the card. Failure to maintain the grade card could result in possible legal action.  15A NCAC 18A .2660 PUBLIC DISPLAY OF GRADE CARDS (a) Upon initial inspection of a food establishment or if a renovation or other change in the establishment makes the grade card inconspicuous; the regulatory authority shall designate the location for posting the grade card. The grade card shall be located in a conspicuous place where it may be readily observed by the public upon entering the food establishment. If the person in charge of the food establishment objects to the location designated by the regulatory authority then the person in charge may suggest an alternative location which meets the criteria of this Rule. (b) When an inspection of a food establishment is made; the regulatory authority shall remove the existing grade card; issue a new grade card; and post the new grade card in the same location where the grade card was previously posted as long as that location remains conspicuous. The person in charge of the food establishment shall keep the grade card posted at the designated location at all times. The grade card may be posted in another location which meets the criteria of this Rule if agreed upon by the person in charge and the regulatory authority.

Serv Safe: 0 When cooling rice or other items; the idea is to do it as quick as possible. After cooking the rice; it should be spread out in a thin layer of no deeper than 2 inches (5 cm). The rice may stay out for a few minutes but when the product has cooled to 135 degrees; you must start cooling the product rapidly by placing it into the walk-in refrigerator. Leave the product uncovered to help it cool faster. After the product has cooled to 41 degrees; you may dump it into a deeper container to save space and put a lid on the product.  Date it with the date it was cooked if it is not used the first day.

Serv Safe: 0 Will return to check written procedure used for time as a public health on hush puppies and to insure that quat test strips are in place. When doing Time as a public health : (A) Except as specified under ¶ (D) of this section; if time without temperature control is used as the public health control for a working supply of POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS FOOD (TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD) before cooking; or for READY-TO-EAT POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS FOOD (TIME/TEMPERATURE CONTROL FOR SAFETY FOOD) that is displayed or held for sale or service:  (1) Written procedures shall be prepared in advance; maintained in the FOOD ESTABLISHMENT and made available to the REGULATORY AUTHORITY upon request that specify: Pf (a) Methods of compliance with Subparagraphs (B)(1)-(3) or C)(1)-(5) of this section; Pf and (b) Methods of compliance with § 3-501.14 for FOOD that is prepared; cooked; and refrigerated before time is used as a public health control. Pf"  (B) If time without temperature control is used as the public health control up to a maximum of 4 hours:  (1) The FOOD shall have an initial temperature of 5°C (41°F) or less; or 7°C (45°F) or less when removed from cold holding temperature control; or 57°C (135°F) or greater when removed from hot holding temperature control; P (2) The FOOD shall be marked or otherwise identified to indicate the time that is 4 hours past the point in time when the FOOD is removed from temperature control; Pf  (3) The FOOD shall be cooked and served; served at any temperature if READY-TO-EAT; or discarded; within 4 hours from the point in time when the FOOD is removed from temperature control; P and (4) The FOOD in unmarked containers or PACKAGES; or marked to exceed a 4-hour limit shall be discarded.

From the 2017 North Carolina Food Code Manual: 3-603.11 Consumption of Animal Foods that are Raw; Undercooked; or Not Otherwise Processed to Eliminate Pathogens.  (A) Except as specified in  3-401.11(C) and Subparagraph 3-401.11(D)(4) and under  3-801.11(C); if an animal FOOD such as beef; EGGS; FISH; lamb; milk; pork; POULTRY; or shellfish is served or sold raw; undercooked; or without otherwise being processed to eliminate pathogens; either in READY-TO-EAT form or as an ingredient in another READY-TO-EAT FOOD; the PERMIT HOLDER shall inform CONSUMERS of the significantly increased RISK of consuming such FOODS by way of a DISCLOSURE and REMINDER; as specified in  (B) and (C) of this section using brochures; deli case or menu advisories; label statements; table tents; placards; or other effective written means.  (B) DISCLOSURE shall include: (1) A description of the animal-derived FOODS; such as “oysters on the half shell (raw oysters);” “raw-EGG Caesar salad;” and “hamburgers (can be cooked to order)”; or (2) Identification of the animal-derived FOODS by asterisking them to a footnote that states that the items are served raw or undercooked; or contain (or may contain) raw or undercooked ingredients.  (C) REMINDER shall include asterisking the animal-derived FOODS requiring DISCLOSURE to a footnote that states: (1) Regarding the safety of these items; written information is available upon request;  (2) Consuming raw or undercooked MEATS; POULTRY; seafood; shellfish; or EGGS may increase your RISK of foodborne illness; or (3) Consuming raw or undercooked MEATS; POULTRY; seafood; shellfish; or EGGS may increase your RISK of foodborne illness; especially if you have certain medical conditions.
